utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are watching us. If there are no procedural matters, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Butler. Welcome back. I hope very much that this is the last time that I have to welcome you back in the courtroom. If I have counted correctly, it's the 16th day that you are with us here in the Court before and after the summer recess. That's really a lot, and we thank you for your patience. Mr. Tolimir is continuing and concluding his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor. And please bear in mind that you have used 23 hours and 17 minutes up to now for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace be with us. Let these proceedings end in keeping with God's will, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also wish to welcome Mr. Butler again in the courtroom. Last time, we were looking at 1D945, and I would like it to be displayed in e-court again. It's a document of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated 23 September 1995. It says Brigadier Naser Oric, information, and indicia. Sent to -- Have you seen this document? Have you reviewed it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know why Naser Oric was in the federation before the operation breakthrough, which he, by the way, had agreed, with the 2nd Corps, and why he was not with the 28th Division when they started their breakthrough? Have you done any research into that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that at some juncture he left the enclave. I believe it was either April or May of 1995. I don't know the specific reason offhand. I have heard a number of stories, but I have never come across the specific reason why he left, and I have not done research on it because it wasn't relevant for what I was doing with respect to the particular topics I was engaged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you come across documents saying that the 28th Division and the units of the 2nd Corps were supposed to meet at Han Pogled, near Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only document that I've seen that reflects that is a -- the document that you showed me, I believe it, on the first or second day of my cross-examination by you which reflects the draft plan that was under consideration by the ABiH for that. I have not seen anything subsequent to that where it's a formal plan or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll show that a bit later. Let's just remove this document from e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at page 2 of this document, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, I quote: [As read] "After the withdrawal of the units of the 28th Division from Srebrenica, Oric, in Tuzla, prohibits the organs of the military security, the making of counter-intelligence assessments for the units of the 28th Division, whereby he practically blocked the operative investigation into the fall of Srebrenica and its causes. In addition, he forbade the members of the 28th Division at the giving of any statements to the organs of the military security of the 2nd Corps or the MUP of the state security department in Tuzla. So most fighting men were reluctant and fearful and spoke very little, if anything, about their observations concerning Oric and his associates." Do you have any knowledge about this -- about these prohibitions he imposed on the members of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at page 6 of this report from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote: [As read] "Naser Oric and Enver Stitkovac from Zepa were taking gold items from the population in exchange for food; for instance, 1 kilo of potatoes in exchange for one golden ring. On the instructions of Naser Oric, Nedzad Bektic took the gold items collected in this way and melted them into small pieces the same size as a pack of cigarettes, approximately, and then melted lead over it. These ingots were seen in the apartment of Oric and Bektic by Safet Omanovic, also known as Mis. The money and the gold, Oric allegedly took by helicopter to Tuzla when he travelled there. Hajro Hasanovic said to our source that Oric is worth 3 to 4 million Deutschmark." Would you say that these mercantile interests of Oric had something to do with his failure to appear with the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I have heard these stories, specifically the one that gold that was supposedly appropriated by Naser Oric was flown out of the enclave by helicopter. So these are well-travelled allegations with respect to how Naser Oric did or did not make his money. I can't speculate as to whether or not that was the reason why he was not in the enclave in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have seen document D145, paragraph 3, let's look at it again. Thank you. D145, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see it in e-court. It's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The paragraph 3 says: [As read] "According to our information, the return of Naser Oric is connected with the planned commencement of operations from the Srebrenica enclave which supposedly is conditioned by the possible taking of the Vis elevation in the Serbian municipality of Kalesija by the Muslim forces from the direction of Kalesija, whereby they would create conditions for further penetration towards municipality of Sekovici. Following this, combat would supposedly begin from the direction Kladanj towards the VRS defence lines in the zone of responsibility of the Vlasenica Brigade when the units of Srebrenica would insert themselves towards Konjevic Polje, the other sector of Buljim in the Milici municipality." Did Muslim units, armed Muslim units, really come out of the Srebrenica enclave, especially in this direction towards Han Pijesak from the direction of Kladanj, as indicated here? It's not recorded that the attack on the Main Staff occurred on the 26th. The attack was mounted by units from the demilitarised areas of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I've discussed, I am aware that during the month of June, a number of military units from Srebrenica and Zepa conducted a series of raids outside the enclave. I am not aware that at the same time that they were doing this that forces from Kladanj were trying to attack towards the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's also look at 1D346 in e-court. We can see it now. It's a document of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, command of the 2nd Corps, sent from Tuzla on 28th June, 1995, addressed to the commands of the 28th Division and the command of the 285th Light Brigade. I am reading from paragraph 2: [As read] "In the period that follows, adhere to orders given so far. Prepare plans for active combat operations for the given moment. You will get orders for further or follow-up combat operations from us or from the Main Staff of the BH Army. Because of problems with the entry of convoys into Zepa and Srebrenica, it is important at this moment to have contingency plans for combat operations but also to wait for more favourable times because of the difficult situation with food for civilians and members of the ABiH for further combat operations outside the zones of Srebrenica and Zepa." My question is: Have you noticed that the command of the 2nd Corps is sending this to the division without ever mentioning the entry of the division or the presence of the division in the area where the combat operations are to take place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I am understanding your question, sir. They are mentioning Srebrenica and Zepa in the third paragraph. Is there another location that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: They are saying that active combat operations would be mounted from the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa. You noted that in your previous answer; correct? If - and the is my question -- if the enclaves decide to mount attacks behind the lines of the VRS, is that practically a declaration of war against the VRS by the demilitarised areas?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree to your terminology only because obviously a state of armed conflict already existed, and certainly with respect to the Srebrenica and Zepa safe areas, they were never demilitarised. Again, in this context, it is not Naser Oric individually who is making decisions on whether to make raids out of the enclave and, to use your phrase, go to war against the VRS. These decisions are being made within a broader military context of what is happen in eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is why I displayed this document, to show that this announcement is made by the 2nd Corps of the BH Army, this document we are looking at now. And they say that these units should start combat operations from Srebrenica and Zepa, but they should wait for the right moment. Have you studied any documents why Naser Oric did not join the division then, and do you know that he was involved in the attack against the VRS from the Zuka Barracks, the attack at Baljkovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I did not study, and I don't why Naser Oric did not rejoin his unit. I am aware that at some point following the fall of Srebrenica, Naser Oric was among some of the officers involved with working with the 24th Infantry Division in attacks against units of the Zvornik Brigade holding the forward lines in an attempt to create a hole for the column to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Butler. My time is running out. Is it logical for the commander of the division to be with the division when they are breaking out of encirclement, and can you think of any reason why he wouldn't be with them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the issues that's out there is not only with respect to Naser Oric but why so many other senior ranking officers and staff members of the 28th Division were also out of the enclave at the same time that Naser Oric was. And those officers were also not available to go or to work with the 28th Division as it was fighting its way out of the enclave after 11 July 1995. Normally, from a military sense, the commander is normally where the majority of his forces are, where he can best exercise command. Obviously, there will be times when the commander is called away for certain functions, it could be training, it could be staff preparation for future offensive activities, there is a variety of reasons. You normally, particularly in a combat operation, would never want to take away so many officers from a unit that it would place that unit at risk if it had to engage in significant combat operations and all of the relevant officers were away from their posts. Again, I don't know why Naser Oric and all of those individual officers were taken from the enclave, and I don't know why they did not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Could it be considered an obstruction of proper defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume you're referring to a military defence as opposed to a legal defence? It -- like I said, when you take that many officers away from a military unit, you are assuming a higher risk. In a defence, obviously, you already generally have well-established plans and things of that nature, but as you saw with the 28th, what started as a defence quickly led to a situation where the Division had to offensively fight its way through 50 kilometres at least of enemy terrain and territory to try and breakout from behind the lines. Those are very dynamic circumstances, and under those circumstances, you know, had those officers been available it would have been to the -- it would have certainly helped the 28th Division. Now, whether it would have changed anything or not is speculation, but going back to what General Tolimir has asked, yeah, it certainly does have a detrimental effect of the military ability of the 28th Infantry Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I have no more time to discuss this issue, but I would just like to ask you: Have you studied statements of other commanding officers of the 28th Division concerning the breakthrough and the reasons why they took so many losses? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender 1D364, 1D945 as well. If they could be admitted into evidence while I move to another subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please explain a little bit further, 1D945, despite the fact -- besides the fact that there is no translation, I don't know if this can be tendered through this witness, Mr. Butler. He clearly stated that he didn't see it before, that he didn't study it, that he couldn't say anything about the content, about the absence or presence of and the conduct of Naser Oric. How can that be admitted through Mr. Butler? Could you explain that? I am referring to 1D945.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness answered, and he said that it had a negative impact on the quality of defence and the organisation of defence of the 28th Division in Srebrenica. He provided a number of other parameters which proved that somebody deliberately took a number of officers from the area of the 28th Division in Srebrenica. It should be admitted for the benefit of the Trial Chamber because it confirms some elements; namely, that there was a deliberate obstruction of the defence of Srebrenica and the division of the column in two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand this is your position, but I was asking about the knowledge and the testimony of Mr. Butler in relation to that document. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both documents will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D945 shall be assigned Exhibit D310.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked for identification, pending translation. And 65 ter document 1D364 shall be assigned Exhibit D311 marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now look at D277 in e-court. D277. This is Hakija Meholjic's interview. He was the president of the War Presidency in Srebrenica, and the interview was given to the Sarajevo newspaper "Dani." Let's look at D277. Now we can see it, and the title is: "5.000 Muslim Lives for Military Intervention." Yesterday, we read the first paragraph -- rather, the second paragraph, the first five lines of it. I don't have much time, so I don't want to waste it, but I would like to say that Meholjic said that Alija Izetbegovic had offered him to sacrifice 5.000 Muslims and that would be a pretext for a NATO intervention. On the second page of the same document - could we please look at it - in the second paragraph, the journalist asks Meholjic: [As read] "After the fall of Srebrenica in 1995, you had a chance to address President Izetbegovic." Meholjic says: [As read] "I requested then that a state commission be formed to examine the responsibility of the international community, the president, the army General Staff, the 2nd Army Corps and their responsibility. The people are missing. He, President Izetbegovic, asked me what I would achieve with that. Rasim Delic tried to say something too, but nobody gave him a chance to speak. I did not interfere, but, General, I have a very bad opinion about the majority of the General Staff members. Never in the history of wars had the people 'processed' by other armies been appointed commanders," so on and so forth. [As read] "You spent five to six months in their prison, and then you come through and exchange and become a commander. On the second day after Srebrenica fell, we heard on the radio in the woods Rasim Delic calling us to return as the situation in Srebrenica was normal."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question: Do you know that Mr. Meholjic, after the fall of Srebrenica, and after the people of Srebrenica came to the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps, asked Alija Izetbegovic about criminal proceedings be issued on account of his statement that 5.000 Muslims should be killed to provoke NATO intervention? My question is: Did you study the plan to kill, or, rather, slaughter the 5.000 Muslims in Srebrenica? Did you study it or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I said yesterday, I cannot speak to what Mr. Meholjic may or may not have said or believed. I am generally aware that throughout the course of the conflict one of the ideas that was always available or brought up was that components of Srebrenica might be traded for areas of the Sarajevo area that were under Bosnian Serb control. I am not aware of any plan to slaughter 5.000 Muslims in Srebrenica by the former president, and as a result I didn't study it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case can we look at D122. This is a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move away from this document, it should stay on the screen. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a question about this exhibit, D277. General Tolimir's question to the witness was whether he was aware of Izetbegovic's plan or idea to slaughter or massacre 5.000 Muslims, and the witness said that he wasn't aware of any such plan. But I am addressing the Defence now: General Tolimir, your document is in B/C/S. I don't have a translations into either English or French -- no, no, there is an English translation, I apologise. But I would like to know whether you have a paragraph where there is an explanation as to how President Izetbegovic wanted to kill 5.000 Muslims in order to provoke a foreign intervention. Is there a passage to that effect that explains that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Mindua. There is. On the first page, we quoted from that paragraph before. Let's go back to the first page. I would kindly ask e-court to go back to the first page. Now we see it. In the second paragraph Meholjic says: "We rejected this without any discussion." This means that he rejected Izetbegovic's offer. And then he said: [As read] "'You know, I was offered by Clinton in April 1993 (after the fall of Cerska and Konjevic Polje) that the Chetnik forces enter Srebrenica, carry out a slaughter of 5.000 Muslims, and then there will be a military intervention.'" We quoted that last time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will do for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I have a question for Mr. Butler, just a clarification so I can understand things better. Your research, you study, did it encompass both sides to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, ma'am. My study was with respect to the activities of the VRS with respect to the fall of Srebrenica and what happened afterwards. It was not designed, and I never offered as such, that it is a total historical re-accounting of everything that went on in eastern Bosnia on both sides that led to those circumstances; that is, as you are aware, many of those developments are political and diplomatic developments that are beyond my expertise to comment on. So my analysis is strictly related to the military issues related to the Army of the Republika Srpska in this context. So while I do have some knowledge of the surrounding ABiH military situation as it was relevant, it only sets the context for what happens afterwards. I did not engage in a study of the ABiH or the 28th Infantry Division, for that matter, in the same detail that I did for the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you, Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did you read the Secretary-General's report entitled: "The Fall of Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In that case, I would like to call up D122, paragraph 115. Thank you. 51 in Serbian, 33 in English. Thank you. Let's look at the page, please. 51 in Serbian, 33 in English, paragraph 115. We can now see the paragraph both in English and in Serbian. I am going to read just the first sentence in that paragraph. [As read] "Representatives of the Bosniak community gathered in Sarajevo on the 28th and 29th September ..." This is just to pin-point the period. And now line 9, where it says, and I quote: [As read] "Some survivors from the Srebrenica delegation stated that President Izetbegovic also told them that there were Serb proposals that he had learned that a NATO intervention in Bosnia and Herzegovina was possible, but could only occur if the Serbs were to break into Srebrenica, killing at least 5.000 of its people. President Izetbegovic has flatly denied making such a statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this, Mr. Butler: In the Secretary-General's report on the fall of Srebrenica, did you see this? Did you ever hear anything about this? Did you ever study this matter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I have read the report. The allegation is listed here. I did not look into this particular allegation as I don't believe it was relevant to the work that I was doing, and so I am not in a position to offer any additional clarification as to whether it did or did not occur or what it may or may not have meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. On the 8th of July, when you testified, on page 16333, lines 8 through 19, you stated the following: [As read] "I believe that the publication of crimes, the number of missing, buried, and killed had a political effect on the willingness of NATO to interfere with the politics of Republika Srpska. In the ensuing months, up to the end of the war, due to the NATO activities and Croatian Operation Storm, the war ended with the Dayton Accords and, as a result of that, Republika Srpska was geographically smaller than it was in July 1995." My question is this: Bill Clinton and Alija Izetbegovic had an idea for NATO to intervene in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did that come to fruition?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak for the former president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I certainly cannot speak for the former president of the United States as to whether or not this was part of a plan or if it even occurred. One of them is dead and one of them can be subpoenaed, I guess. You can ask him that particular question. I have no ability to comment on it one way or another, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Could you please tell us whether there was a NATO intervention against Republika Srpska, as you described in here in August, September, October, up to the signing of the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that I left in order to participate in the defence against the NATO intervention? I went to Zepa and Drvar. Did you see documents? Did you hear the testimonies of witnesses to that effect? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the general could just be clear that he left "what"? We can't tell from the English translation where he left, and I don't think Mr. Butler should have to speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- could you add this information to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I was in Zepa. Did I leave to defend the Republika Srpska against the aggressions mounted by Croatia and NATO in the western part of Republika Srpska, in Drvar and the surrounding areas? Did you read documents about that? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again sir, as I have testified, I did not research your specific movements within the VRS after Zepa. I know that while you say you left to go to Drvar, I mean, but the reality is that you didn't displace yourself. You were just performing your duties in a different location. You did not leave the Main Staff. You were always still the assistant commander of intelligence and security. The fact that you may be performing your duties in a different location of the Republika Srpska where the threat is more acute at the moment, in my mind, is not the equivalent of saying that you left and did something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. It is neither here nor there. That was not even my question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at D187. We can see a report where it says in the first sentence of the report sent by the Rogatica Brigade on the 30th of August, 1995. I quote -- this is a regular combat report. It says: [As read] "This morning, around 0230 hours, NATO aviation bombarded facilities that had housed the communications centre at Zlovrh feature. The feature had been torched by the Ustashi, and over the past ten days it had been used to billet our units that scared the terrain." There is a reference to the number killed. It says that a total number of casualties was 14. I don't have anymore time. Therefore, I would like to move to another document, 1D617, on a similar topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But let me ask you first: Fire opened on Zepa, did that fit in with NATO aviation intervention? Could UNPROFOR open fire there or could it just be NATO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In that context you would be talking about NATO orchestrated air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at 1D769 now. And while we are waiting for the document to appear on the screen, I would like to say that this is a document issued by the Main Staff of the VRS on the 26th of December, 1995. The title is: "Casualties and Damages as a Result of NATO Bombing." And this was sent to the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. It says here: [As read] "In order to possibly pay compensation for property damages as a result of NATO bombing and rapid intervention force in the course of September of this year, here enclosed, please find a list of killed and wounded citizen of the Republika Srpska." This document was signed by commander Ratko Mladic. It has several pages on which it says 37 VRS members were killed, 73 were wounded, and there is a list from 1 through 73. There is a list of names. There is also a reference to those who were killed but were not members of the VRS, 1 through 5. And we don't want to actually dwell upon all that. At the end, General Ratko Mladic signed that, stamped it, and sent it to the General Staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this, sir: The consequences of NATO bombing and the consequences of rapid intervention forces activities, did they also include consequences of UNPROFOR intervention or were they exclusively the result of NATO intervention? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO bombing and forces were clearly NATO air assets. Some forces that were part of the UNPROFOR were -- who were already in country, my understanding was that they were redesignated to be part of a NATO rapid reaction force, which, if it occurred at that way, would definitely blur the line between forces that were formally the UNPROFOR and who were now taking a more active role in the conflict as part of a NATO rapid reaction force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, there is a reference to a NATO intervention as well as to NATO rapid reaction forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at 1D -- D193.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document to appear, let me tell you that this is a statement by Mr. Rupert Smith. He provided it on the 14th of August, 1996. My question to you, sir, is this: Do you know that at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, let me interrupt you for a moment. Sorry for interrupting you. You used 1D769, the report of Mr. Mladic. Are you tendering that document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D769 -- correction, 1D769, shall be assigned Exhibit D312, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Butler, is: In August, September, and October, and all the way until the signing of the Dayton Accords, did the UNPROFOR have a mandate in Bosnia and Herzegovina to keep peace or to enforce peace, according to the relevant resolutions of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR mandate was obviously a peacekeeping mandate. But as I said previously, with the NATO intervention, as you use the phrase, that occurred in August, September, October, particularly with respect to the rapid reaction forces, many of the military forces that were previously part of the UNPROFOR were redesignated as part of the rapid reaction forces -- or, I shouldn't say many, but certainly some of the more capable ones, and as a result the line gets blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, these rapid reaction forces and NATO forces, did they have a mandate to impose peace in Bosnia by using armed force and by taking the side of one of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the mandate of the rapid reaction force was to apply military force against the VRS forces and against the Republika Srpska in order to force them - I guess that's probably the best word in this case -- force them to comply with previous United Nations resolutions regarding -- and the agreements regarding the -- I guess it's the 20-kilometre zone around Sarajevo and the agreement to place all their heavy weaponry under international observation so it can't be used for shelling Sarajevo. That is my understanding of what the goal of the rapid reaction force, as well as what the NATO bomb campaign was designed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We see now the statement of General Smith, the UN force commander.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see page 15 in English, the last paragraph, and page 16 in Serbian, paragraph 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's see what he says about the mandate of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if I refer you to your last question, you are now dealing with matters you have already dealt with in an earlier part of your cross-examination. As I told you, you should conclude your cross-examination within the first session of today. Now you have had the opportunity to use the same amount of time as the Prosecution did. You may have some more minutes, but please try to come to an end. The best way is to avoid any repetition. Your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am quoting from Rupert Smith's statement about their mandate, paragraph 5 in Serbian, and the last paragraph in English: [As read] "Sarajevo remained under siege and the airport closed. A decision was taken within the UN that that for the time being, the force would continue to operate peacekeeping principles. Plans that I had developed to use a degree of force to resupply Sarajevo via the Igman route and to use helicopters to supply fuel to the enclaves where the supply situation was worsening were not accepted by our headquarters in Zagreb." My question is: Is it obvious from this that UNPROFOR's mandate was to keep peace and that decision was made by the UN Security Council, yes or no, or were they free to act at will?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Smith's statement in that regard deals -- it deals with his view in June of 1995 with respect to the UN mandate and the decisions that were made in this case over his head by the headquarters in Zagreb. How that evolved through the month of July and August of 1995, I believe is well documented in the United Nations report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you cite any resolution that allowed the use of force in Republika Srpska? Did you hold such a resolution in your hands?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never held any resolution in my hands with that respect, and I am not familiar with a United Nations Security Council resolution specifically authorising a use of force in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Can you tell us whether both UNPROFOR and NATO and the Croatian Army and also the ABiH are allies against VRS? At this moment, I am talking about August, September, October, all the way up to the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that in August and September and October and through the Dayton Accords, the UNPROFOR, NATO, the Croatian Army, and the ABiH, were all engaged in military operations, to one degree or another, against the Republika Srpska and, specific, the VRS. I don't know that I could specifically tell you whether they were allies in that sense or whether or not that they were operating as some part of a larger shared plan or intent. I believe that other witnesses in other trials, specifically, have given their opinions on those issues, and I am speaking specifically of Mr. Holbrooke, as to what the big picture was because he was a part of it. That would be the most appropriate person to ask that question to. I couldn't comment on it anymore than I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Since you mention Mr. Holbrooke, did you see in that report that he was issuing tasks to NATO, which towns in Republika Srpska they were to capture and to conquer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I am not familiar with the details of his testimony. I am not familiar with a lot of those reports, as you call them, and I have not read his book, so I am just not in a position to lay out what he did or did not do or is accused of doing in any more detail that I have just given.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In that case, let's only look at D122 to see what Mr. Holbrooke says. Page 101 in English, page 183 in Serbian, paragraph 461. Just one quotation, because I don't have much time: [As read] "The United States continued its efforts to modulate the military situation on the ground. Writing after the event, Mr. Holbrooke recalled a meeting with President Tudjman of Croatia on September 17. He says, 'I told Tudjman that the Croatian offensive had great value to the negotiations. It would be much easier to retain at the table what had been won on the battle-field than to get the Serbs to give up territory controlled -- they have controlled for several years. I urged Tudjman to take Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Bosanski Novi, all important towns," et cetera, et cetera. I have no more time. They are now part of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, these towns. Is it the case that Richard Holbrooke, as a negotiator and a cosignatory of the Dayton Accords, gave tasks to the Croatian Army and NATO which parts of Republika Srpska territory to carve out so that his own situation at the negotiating table would be better? Did he indeed play had a leading role in the negotiating process which resulted in the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's easier to answer the second question first, which is, yes, he did, obviously, as history notes. As to your first question, what this particular report says is what it says. If you need additional information on that, I -- I said I can't offer anymore than what I've seen in the report which I suspect either they interviewed him or cited his book. It is what it is. I just don't have any amplifying information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just one more passage, paragraph 462, where Mr. Holbrooke speaks precisely about those maps that he was drawing. He says, in paragraph 462: [As read] "Until the end of July, the Bosnian Serbs had controlled approximately 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. By 22 September, UNPROFOR assessed that the Serbs controlled approximately 49 per cent of the country, while the federation partners controlled approximately 51 per cent between them (approximately 30 per cent for the Bosniaks and 21 per cent for the Croats). The map of the battle-field broadly resembled the territorial arrangements being proposed by the United States team." My question is: Is it the case that the operations mounted by NATO and the Croatian forces and the ABiH all focus on achieving this situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, the military operations by the various parties had individual goals. I mean, the Croatian force's goal was the liberation of territory that they believe was integral to the Republic of Croatia. The ABiH was liberating territory that it believed was occupied by the VRS. NATO's goal was as I've discussed before. But it's -- you know, again, as history notes, those three particular goals, you know, did serve to roll back the territory that was under the control of the Republika Srpska to a juncture that the negotiating parties believed was fair for all sides. Now, whether that was done as part of a master plan or whether it just turned out that way is a question beyond my ability to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Please, if we bear in mind this partnership or this alliance, call it what you want, between NATO, UNPROFOR, the Croatian Army, and the BH Army, my question is: Did UNPROFOR members consciously tolerate the arming of supposedly demilitarised areas of Srebrenica and Zepa so that at the time of the intervention they would have armed forces behind the lines of the VRS, forces that they could activate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the first segment of your question, the answer is certainly the UNPROFOR was aware that the ABiH was not demilitarised in neither Zepa or Srebrenica, so I guess that would check the box for consciously tolerate. As for their motive, I can't talk to the motive of what various UNPROFOR leaders were and were not doing and what they were thinking. It's just beyond by competence to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to be very clear, you have ten minutes left, and then you should conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Last time in your closing argument you were saying something about what Tolimir knew or should have known. Could he have been involved in Srebrenica at all if he was elsewhere protecting Republika Srpska from an aggression that lasted a long time, all the way up to the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events with respect to Srebrenica occurred in July of 1995 prior to the period when you claim that you went to the Krajina area or other parts of Bosnia. Whether the -- I am not sure if it's even a Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the second part of your question is that even after that time, you were still the assistant commander for intelligence and security for the entire VRS, the fact that you are not present at the headquarters of the Main Staff, does not mean that you do not have the ability to find out what is going on or to issue orders relevant to those types of issues; again, as we discussed, the prisoner issue. The fact that you were not physically at the Main Staff headquarters does not deprive you of the ability to know of all these things nor, in my opinion, the responsibility to deal with them when you find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Let's see if that was possible to find out, because I was in a different theater of war, not in the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see D526. D526.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting -- and that's a letter from Colonel Jankovic, dated 13 July, 1995, whereby he informs that the evacuation of the entire Muslim population from the former enclave of Srebrenica had been completed. And you spoke about that in your examination-in-chief. Colonel Jankovic writing to the headquarters of the staff, the Main Staff, I didn't see it but other people did, he says in the last paragraph: [As read] "I believe that if we want to take over the enclaves of Zepa and Gorazde in the same way, it will be necessary to present the operation in Srebrenica in the media to show that we had given adequate treatment to the civilians and even to soldiers who had surrendered their weapons." This report by Jankovic, does it indicate that he was not aware of this report of the 12th, because he's planning to present things to the media in quite a different way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, this is not D526 but P626. There is no document with the number D526 in this trial. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe he's asking Mr. Butler to compare this document and Colonel Jankovic's knowledge with a document from the 12th. And if that's the case, it would only be fair to see that document and which part of that document on the 12th he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not referring to the 12th, Mr. McCloskey. I am referring to your claim that the killing plan was made on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am asking if this report made by Jankovic fits with that idea, that the plan to kill was made on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I have testified before on this particular document and that issue, I believe that that final paragraph is not a reflection of the fact that Colonel Jankovic does not know. I believe it's a reflection of the fact that Colonel Jankovic is aware of what's going on and would have been, from his location at Bratunac, and that his suggestion relates not to what is really happening but, more importantly, how to portray the situation in the media in order to get the most favourable results for the VRS with respect to the enclaves of Zepa and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. That's your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D298.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see a decree by the president of Republika Srpska, pursuant to Article 80 of the constitution of Republika Srpska and Article 369 of the army -- of the Law on the Army. The following VRS officers are hereby sent to retirement and transferred to the reserve force: Milan Gvero, Djordje Djukic, Grujo Boric and Zdravko Tolimir. You tried to portray me as somebody who is able to appoint and replace other officers during the NATO intervention. Could I really have done that, because we see from this that I was retired at the time and transferred to the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, I did not make the statement that you said I did: Has the ability to appoint and replace officers during the NATO intervention. Secondly, sir, as you are aware, ultimately this decision by President Karadzic was rescinded. You know, the officers in question remained on active duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did these officers remain actively in service or were they transferred to the reserve force? Can a general remain a general in the reserve force, be a military conscript and keep the same rank?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as you're aware, particularly with respect to the authority of the civilian leadership over the military, on 3 August 1995, President Karadzic sought to appoint General Mladic to a different position, as opposed to his role as the commander of the Main Staff. And on subsequent days, a large section, or almost all of the active generals of the Army of the Republika Srpska published a letter basically calling for the military to ignore that order and throwing your support behind General Mladic. So, again, regardless of where you are in the Republika Srpska, you certainly have the ability to participate in the relevant events that are occurring. This particular document is a reflection of President Karadzic and the SDS not being particularly happy with your decisions with respect to the support of General Mladic. And, again, as you are aware, this order was ultimately rescinded and you remained at your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, thank you. My last question: Do you mean the decision from August or do you mean this decision here, the one we are looking at now from October, not August?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that both decisions were ultimately rescinded, and, to my knowledge, you remained the assistant commander for intelligence and security for the VRS until you were relieved in November 1996 by then-President Plavsic [Realtime transcript read in error "Pilavcic"] as well as all of the other officers who were then on the Main Staff, or most of them, I should say. A few survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, page 30, line 12, the name on the record is "Pilavcic," and that's what I heard in Serbian as well. Was that a slip of the tongue in English or was it just wrongly recorded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, could you please repeat the name of the then-president.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ms. Biljana Plavsic. Hopefully I am pronouncing that correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have it now on the screen correctly. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, and under the decision of Biljana Plavsic, was I transferred from Republika Srpska to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Rather than being retired, was I transferred from the VRS to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now finally really the last question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question, sir. I can't say that I have actually seen the November 1996 order related to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. That doesn't really matter at all, but it's important, speaking of documents, to show that there are documents of both kinds. Thank you for testifying. I wish you good health and a safe return home. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has completed its examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have our first break now, and we will resume with the re-examination by Mr. McCloskey at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it is my hope that this poor witness may leave today. That means that you conclude your re-examination in the course of today's hearing, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is my extreme hope as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, General Tolimir, at page 17390, brought up the 15 July intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could bring up that intercept, I believe it's confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If -- and that is the 15 July conversation between Colonel Beara calling General Krstic requesting more troops and, in your analysis, to take care of the remaining executions in the area of Zvornik Brigade. And General Tolimir asked you at page 17392, when referring to this: "Mr. Butler, how could General Tolimir know anything if he was unable to read any documents and he had not received any calls from the participants directly involved in these problems?" And you respond in part: "General Tolimir obviously had a means to communicate on a variety of levels to individuals who were involved in this." Now, can you remind us on the 15th of July --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we have that document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you remind us on the 15th of July if you recall what General Krstic was doing and where -- where he was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of July at the time of this particular intercept, which is 1000 hours, General Krstic is at the Drina Corps forward command post, the IKM, I believe it's in the village of Kravica, if I pronounced it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we've got Kravica. How about, I think we talked about it before, Krivace? Does that sound familiar/similar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the correct pronunciation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what operation, if any, was he involved in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he was directing the Drina Corps's attack against the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on 15 July, do you recall from the documents where or what operation General Tolimir was involved in and where he was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir was involved in the same operation. I believe on the 15th of July he was located at the forward command post of the Rogatica Brigade. If I recall correctly, it's Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 2555 [Realtime transcript read in error "2255"].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'll see as this comes up, just to try to save some time, that it's from -- up in the left-hand corner, the -- sorry, it's 2555. And it should be, if the correct one comes up, a document from the Drina Corps command dated 15 July. And it says: "Forward command post Krivace," and it's to the Main Staff in the Drina Corps command, and it's an extraordinary combat report in the name of General Krstic. And does this support your conclusion that on the 15th of July General Krstic was at Krivace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, among other information that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2555 shall be assigned Exhibit P2572. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can we briefly go to P129.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which you'll see is from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade that we know as the Rogatica Brigade dated 15 July. It's a teleprinter document in the name of Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. And does this document support your conclusion about the whereabouts of General Tolimir on 15 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document is dated 14 July, but I believe at the time that he is still there on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We have got a number mix-up. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I meant to have P129 up. I misspoke. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we've got this one up, and so you've concluded this supports your view that he is there on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to P479.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is the one I had previously mentioned, the 15 July, but same question: Does this support your conclusion about his location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, this particular document is dated 15 July, 1995, type signed under his signature, and it's from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade so that would put him in and around the area of the command post of the Rogatica Brigade, whether it's the main command post or the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can we now go to P394B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This should be an intercept, and I believe you have spoken to it already, so I will brief onto this point --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a confidential exhibit. It should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's dated 16 July, 1000 hours, between Mico and Toso. And according to this, a short way down, Toso states that: He can call Uran on the same line that you are communicating with Uran and he can relay the telegram for me through it and you know my call-sign. Can you remind us who Toso is and what Uran was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that we do not have the correct page in Serbian displayed in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be the one at 1000 hours, and we may need to go -- I think he's correct, we need to go down the report so we get the one at 1000 hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Toso is a nickname for General Tolimir, and Uran was call-sign for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember specifically what part of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be their IKM, the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the fact of this intercept that General Tolimir is speaking over this intercept and talking about communicating via Uran, as we've seen in the first line, because the other one is not secure -- excuse me, this one is not secure, does this support what you said earlier, that General Tolimir did have means to communicate with the Drina Corps, General Krstic, and others, in a secure manner?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he could communicate with them both on the unsecure lines as well as in a secure manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, did the VRS use couriers, basically men taking messages back and forth?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And last document on this topic, 65 ter 2580.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document from the command of the Drina Corps Krivace IKM dated 16 July. And I think we can just look at the Serbian version, we see that this is under the name of Major-General Krstic. And where would this indicate General Krstic was on 16 July, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that it's coming from the forward command post, the IKM, it would be my opinion that this is evidence that shows that General Krstic is still at the IKM in Krivace on 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2580 shall be assigned Exhibit P2573. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And my next topic would be going to the area that I think both the Prosecution and General Tolimir spent some time on, and that was the area regarding UNPROFOR and humanitarian convoys into the enclaves and the state commission's responsibility and the VRS's responsibility and the review and overview and various authorisations related to those convoys. And in particular General Tolimir asked you at page 17162, onto the following page: "Mr. Butler, can you tell me when you were reviewing the documents relating to the convoys, did you come across any document testifying to the fact that the Main Staff failed to act in accordance with the decisions of the state committee and that it acted contrary to the decisions when it came to humanitarian convoys?" And you responded: "I don't recall that I did, off the top of my head." And then you described the general process: "As I understand it was -- the committee would, once they approved the convoy, would pass the material onto the Main Staff where they would ultimately clear the convoy for travel. There may have been cases where that has occurred, but I don't recall any, off the top of my head." All right. Since we are dealing with the Main Staff and the commission, can you remind us what kind of body the commission was, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the commission was primarily a civilian body appointed by the Republika Srpska leadership whose job it was, was to co-ordinate on behalf of the civilian organs of the Republika Srpska issues related to the humanitarian organisations that were operating in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so given that our issue, as presented and discussed with you and the general for quite a while, has to do with that body and the VRS, I would like to take us back very briefly to Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which is P1214. And the part I want is the -- under -- should be page 14 in e-court in the English and B/C/S page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to remind us of this language, near the end of the document, but can you remind us who drafted this document, Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drafted by then-Colonel Miletic, who was the chief of operations for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you have testified and the Court understands how this document was put together by the military, and we see that it's in the name of Radovan Karadzic. So the section I want to remind us of related to convoys is: "The relevant state and military organs ..." We see this as -- yes, that paragraph that's identified by the cursor: "... responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restricted issuing of permits reduce and limit logistics support ..." And I won't go on reading it. We can all read it and we've heard it many times. So in your view in looking at this paragraph, is the civilian body -- well, is the civilian government of Radovan Karadzic involved in any way with the army when it comes to this particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They would be. They are the state organs. Whether or not individual members of the commission would see this document is debatable or were even told that it existed, but certainly the individuals who appointed them - the highest levels of government - would know what the goal is and would be either through the witting or unwitting control of that state organ applying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to P689 which is out of the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's an Article 6 that General Tolimir directed you to, which -- we see this Gazette was dated 14 March 1995. And we would like to go to Article 6 that -- just mentions that: [As read] "The permits for the movement of convoys and employees of the UN and humanitarian organisations on the territory of Republika Srpska shall be issued by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian operations, pursuant to committee decisions." All right. So that I believe you agreed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, I see Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, again we don't have the correct page in Serbian. I believe that we should be on the following page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have it now on the screen. Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe you agreed with the general that this was the co-ordinating body for the humanitarian operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now could we go a bit further in the Gazette. And it should be page 3 in the English, and I am told page 3 in the B/C/S. This is dated March 14th as well. And we can see that it says pursuant to Article 80, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it talks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you help us. Where on the B/C/S version we will find that document? Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. And we will need to go up a bit in the B/C/S, there is a number of individuals named there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In any event, we see that this is the decision on the appointment of the president, deputy president, and members of the state committee for co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations. Is this the -- in your view, the committee that was just referred to in the previous article?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see the members on it. And do you see any members of the VRS Main Staff that are actually on this body?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the English translation, the first page of it, number 7, Colonel Djordjic [Realtime transcript read in error "Dzurdzic"], I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall what his position on the Main Staff was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that he was an officer who was involved in dealing with issues related to the UNPROFOR as well as other humanitarian organisations. I believe his name came up in concert with the ICRC issue that came up on the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the other six here, do you recognise any of them as military folks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if they are civilian -- or, political people, and we have a -- we see a colonel from the Main Staff, what can you say, if anything, about the potential workings of this co-ordinating body and its either communication with or influence of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that -- there at least was, by virtue of having Colonel Djordjic, a mechanism by which the Main Staff could keep apprised of all of the discussions related to what that humanitarian body was doing so they had a way of keeping informed. I would also note that that Professor Nikola Koljevic as if deputy president of the Republika Srpska, when I testified before about, you know, whether or not all of the members of the commission would know about what the ultimate goal of Directive 7 was, while individual members of the commission may not, as the deputy president of the Republika Srpska, he is certainly somebody who should have been very familiar with what was really supposed to happen under Directive 7, 7(1).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 41, line 20, there has been an error in spelling. Instead of a Z, there should be a letter J, so Colonel Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so when you say Koljevic should really know what was -- what did you mean by "really know"? Could you just spell that out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a very senior leader of the Republika Srpska, he would have been one of the individuals who would have seen Directive 7 and would be familiar with the goals and objectives behind Directive 7. Arguably, other civilians on the commission might not have been high enough within the scope of the government to be privy to that document. But, again, as the ultimate president of the state committee, he certainly would have by virtue of his role as the deputy president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, could we next go to 65 ter 7516.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document that we have recently identified, so it did not have a 65 ter number, but it -- I think it's helpful in response to the issues that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have an objection to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This may be added to the 65 ter exhibit list, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, this is a -- well, just take a look at it. You can see in the English that it's from the Republika Srpska government co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid. And if I could just give Mr. Butler a hard copy, that may be helpful, and there is a B/C/S for Mr. Gajic as well, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Usher, yes, please, do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could go to page 2 in the English briefly so everyone can see that. We see that this document from the body is in the name of -- its President Dragan Kekic. Okay. So if we could go back to the first page. And it notes, as we see in the English, that permission is given for a request number and it talks about various numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now if we could -- I'm sorry, just to make this clear, if we could go to B/C/S page 3 and English page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll see attached to this document is a document from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, out of an abundance of caution, can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- attract your attention to a note that we see under the second paragraph that -- it states on this document that: [As read] "A weekly plan is hereby approved with the exception of note 3 on the page 3 as printed: "A satellite telex with equipment for use by the UNHCR office." Now, so we see what this document says. We see what the government or the co-ordinating body has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this into evidence, and I have another document relating to it that I want to base my question on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we hear your question and the answer first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My next question is a document that cites this particular document and makes reference to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is 65 ter 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you can see that this document is now dated 19 May, two days after the previous document which was 17 May. And this is from the familiar group of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. And it's to the command of the Drina Corps. And it's a notification to the Drina Corps, and we see in that front page, and I quote: "We have approved request number 1179-HCR-783." So can you -- this particular document, Mr. Butler, can you tell us just what it is in relation to the last document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This appears to be the notification by the Main Staff to the Drina Corps and to the East Bosnian Corps letting them know that they -- they are clearing a particular UN convoy, or a series of convoys, coming into the Republika Srpska, and this is, as I've discussed before, to -- this was the notification to the military about these convoys so they would know when these convoys would be arriving and what they would be carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we now go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, before we go to page 4, can you give us your brief conclusion on whether or not this shows anything to do with the VRS working with the co-ordinating body on these issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, they would have to work in partnership on these issues because even though the co-ordinating body was in their purview to approve or disprove UNHCR convoys, ultimately the Main Staff controlled access to the roads that were particularly related to where the battles were ongoing and that the Main Staff had to be co-ordinated with, fully, otherwise the convoys would not be permitted to enter through any military zone, and they needed to be inspected, and they would be inspected by the military members in those zones. So they obviously were closely co-ordinated in that regard for the maximum amount of efficiency. You just couldn't have a situation where the co-ordinating body was making unilateral decisions and that the Main Staff people who had to transmit these clearances down to the subordinate corps would be unaware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to page 4 in the English. I believe it's page 3 in the B/C/S. It's right above the signature block for Manojlo Milovanovic. And we have a note under of -- or above Milovanovic's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says: "We have not approved the transport of a satellite telex with accompanying equipment to Srebrenica on 24 May." Now this appears to be the same reference that the co-ordinating body had -- did not approve. So, in this case, is the Main Staff doing anything on their own or going against the co-ordinating body in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, this reflects the fact that -- I mean, he's using the phrase "we" collectively for the Republika Srpska, not the Main Staff or the co-ordinating body. So it's a unified decision to allow the corps to know that if they find, you know, satellite communications equipment, that it should be confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. President, I would offer both these last two 65 ter numbers into evidence. I think this would set out an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 65 ter 7516 will be received first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7516 shall be assigned Exhibit P2574. And 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And 65 ter 1946 will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And shall be assigned Exhibit P2575. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Butler. And you were -- on the same topic, you were questioned and you answered several times about the restrictions on humanitarian aid and personnel, and so I wanted to show you 65 ter 1955.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record this is Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P2569. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
