utterances.text: And in any event, we will let that get up on the screen, Mr. Butler. You will see it's from the Main Staff dated 12 June, 1995, to the Drina Corps, in the name of General Miletic. And basically, it states that they agree with the authorisation of MSF, and then it gives the numbers. But then it goes down to the bottom and reiterates that: [As read] "In other words, no foreign MSF officials shall be allowed to enter the enclaves, except for, perhaps, drivers who will transfer the above-mentioned persons to Belgrade." How does this fit into your analysis about personnel or -- or being allowed out or into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's just more information that supports the broader pattern which was occurring was that -- is part of their operation against the enclaves -- or their preparations against the enclaves, I should say, what they were doing was limiting the capacities of the outside organisations. One of the ways that they were doing this was by allowing for individuals leaving the enclaves to leave, from both the Dutch Battalion as well as the humanitarian organisations. But what they were not doing was permitting those individuals to be replaced. So particularly over time, you know, as military officers and soldiers and civilians from the humanitarian organisations would complete their tour, for whatever reason, they would of course be allowed to leave the enclaves, but their replacements would not be allowed to enter the enclaves. The predictable result was that with this drain of personnel both the Dutch Battalion and the humanitarian organisations became less and less capable of performing their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I want to go on to another area where General Tolimir questioned you at length about his various responsibilities and duties. And on page 17311, he quoted you from one of those rules from D202, from the Rules on Land Corps Forces on Peacetime. And on that page he read it out as stating: "The organs of command may not assign their powers to other command organs or transfer their responsibility to the organs of a lower command unless specifically authorised to do so. "My question --" now the question he was asking you as he states: "My question is: In view of this stipulation, could General Tolimir be held responsible for what was in the purview of lower-ranking units, corps, and brigades, and were they able to transfer to him affairs that were within their area of responsibility which would make him answerable for what they were supposed to be responsible for?" Now, I want you to take a look, if you could -- and you do have a long answer for that, but at -- 65 ter 5891. And this is another document that is about five pages in English, and I think we have a -- no, we don't. Well, I will try to just go over it slowly so you and the -- everyone can get a view of it. It's dated 6 of July from the Drina Corps command, security department. And I'll tell you at the end, it's in the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic. And it is entitled: "The Work of the Military Police Check-Points and Instructions." And then it says -- if we could go back to the first page, thanks. And I will just go over the high points as briefly as I can to see if this helps answer the question that the general asked you or that he related. Colonel Popovic is referencing an instruction from the Main Staff of 4 July on the work of the military police. And we can see that there is -- he says: "In spite of a range of measures taken and orders and instructions and guide-lines issued for the establishment," basically noting a lack of understanding and problems. And then he basically copies the instructions. And we see at the bottom of the English: "Instructions for the Work of the Military Police at Check-Points." And if we could go to the next page in the English, this -- and I think we can just briefly scan these instructions. It -- we can see that it's talking about various subjects, including foreign citizens, foreign journalists, Serbs living abroad, crossings in and out. And if we could go to the last page, it should be B/C/S page 4, English page 5. I'm sorry, in my scanning I skipped a section under: "... the same shall apply to international humanitarian and other organisations." So these instructions have to do with that as well. And then we have a note marked E on that page 5 of the English and should be seen in the B/C/S as well: [As read] "Those responsible for the consistent implementation of this instruction and acting in accordance with it shall be the assistant for security of intelligence of the Main Staff, corps commanders ... and their subordinate organs and military police units." So what does this -- and then under that it's commander Ratko Mladic, and then under that we see that the final signature is Popovic after he's copied the whole instruction from General Mladic. Can you just very briefly, very briefly, what, if anything, does this tell us about General Tolimir's responsibility in these particular areas and working with other members as noted here by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, it illustrates that the issue of command and the issue of, you know, technical expertise and advice within the military service, or the VRS specifically, is closely intertwined. It's not designed to be separate or compartmentalised. General Ratko Mladic as the commander of the Main Staff, you know, knows that the assistant for security and intelligence of the Main Staff of the VRS or the primary technical organ which covers the details of how these things are to be done, and he's directing that his subordinate corps commanders as well as their subordinate organs of the military police units, you know, work with them on these particular issues. You know, take advantage of their technical expertise and follow their technical guidance. The whole command and staff process is interrelated. It's not designed to be separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5891 shall be assigned Exhibit P2576. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask Mr. McCloskey and the witness to slow down a little. The interpretation is lagging a little bit behind, so I would kindly ask them to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Going on to another topic that the general spent a fair amount of time on, and that is his questions about restricting UNPROFOR supplies and its effect on UNPROFOR and restricting civilian aid and that affect on the civilians. He asked at page 17190 in referencing a document, 65 ter 05170, he says: "You spoke of various restrictions imposed on UNPROFOR convoys that wants to bring in supplies. Tell us, was the population in any way adversely affected by the restrictions that the VRS may have applied in respect of UNPROFOR convoys?" And the next page, he asks you: "Had there ever been any fatality among the civilian population because of the shortage of medical supplies?" And he asked you if you'd seen any documents that had any such information. And as you may recall, you cited to him, among other things, the UN report, which is D122.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want to go briefly to that to see if what I have found -- yeah, if we could just go to the first page of that so we can see if it's that report that we are all getting familiar with. Thank you. And now if we could go to -- it should be page 56 in the English and B/C/S page 93. And I'm interested in paragraphs 233, 234, and 235.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't want to read them all out. I think we just can all read them ourselves briefly, but you can see that 233 -- when it's the BSA we know that they are referring to Bosnian Serb army. It talks about tightening the squeeze in the safe area, progressively limiting the already restricted flow of humanitarian aid into the enclave and constraining the provision of supplies to DutchBat. It goes on. Then to 234, the DutchBat commander expressed the exasperation at the humanitarian situation. He stated that the warehouse in the enclave would be empty within days. He goes on into more detail. And then 235 talks about not being allowed to leave the enclave and that there had been no food delivered in March, no fresh dairy products, and he goes on into detail. When you referred the general, generally, in response to these questions, had you read this part of the report and did these sections have anything to do with your answer to the general?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I had read the report and I am familiar with these sections of the report. That's why with respect to my basis of knowledge of what happened in the humanitarian aspect within the enclaves is drawn in large part from the UN's own report on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we now go to 65 ter 482. And that's -- if we could blow that up a little bit in both languages, we see that it's an 11 July report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you make out who is writing this report, who it's to, who is writing it, just from your review of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNMO headquarters, BH Sector North-East, so that would be Tuzla, to BH command in Sarajevo, as well as the UN HQ command in Zagreb. And it's a retransmital of a situation report for Srebrenica, presumably drafted by the UN military observers in Srebrenica on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Is this a document you recall reviewing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we look at it again, I won't read all of it, but it talks about a stream of refugees still come into the compound of DutchBat, the food situation is hopeless. For the battalion we have food for a few days. It's impossible to give any food to the refugees. Only water we can supply. The situation will be separate in 48 hours. And at the end, we see: [As read] "DutchBat can't give much help because their supplies are not coming in since the end of April." And the only medical help is from MSF. And so does this help answer the general's question to you about documents that are related to how the restrictions on DutchBat may have affected the civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, it helped over the prior months to create the circumstances where, by the time you got to July of 1995, there were no reserves supplies left for the battalion. There were no reserve supplies left for UNHCR. And then when the military attack started and the population began to move out of Srebrenica, they were showing up at Potocari, placing themselves directly under the protection of the United Nations organisation as well as the Dutch who had no ability to feed them or to provide any sort of comprehensive medical care because they simply did not have the supplies to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 482 shall be assigned Exhibit P2577. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, do you recall reviewing the BiH Army documents that were sent out from Srebrenica in those last few days of the fall of the enclave after the 4th, the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th? Do you remember? Can you go way back? When did you actually review that material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did review that particular group of material. I believe some of them are referenced in my narrative because what the ABiH military leadership in Srebrenica was doing and saying on those particular days is relevant to what the VRS was doing on those particular days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, that answer just reminds me of the question Judge Nyambe asked you regarding the scope of your investigation. You've testified here that your view -- you concluded that the enclave was not demilitarised, that the Muslims were coming out of the enclave at the relevant period of time, attacking Serb -- the Serbs, that the UN did not or was not able to stop this, and that, as such, you felt that that was a fair military target, and other items directly related to the Muslim army and other issues. Have those conclusions that you talked to, did you reach those -- at what level -- at what point, excuse me, in your investigation in your work here in the Tribunal did you come to those conclusions? Was it after trials, prior to trials? Did you reach them on your own? Were you affected by anyone? Can you just very briefly tell us when you came up with those issues that we tend to agree with General Tolimir on that are directly related to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of those opinions were formed by me before General Krstic was even indicted. As I did my research from arriving here in April of 1997, so by June or July of 1997 I was more or less working full time with respect to the Srebrenica investigation. The issues, the Dutch Battalion's reports, even the limited information we had at that time all supported that particular conclusion. As we received additional information, particularly the ABiH documents from the 28th Infantry Division, which we found at the headquarters of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, because apparently when the units of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade captured the enclave -- or their part of the enclave, they were the ones who went through and confiscated various CD -- I thought they were floppy disks, that we ultimately ended up seizing in 1998. They were in the possession of the Zvornik Brigade which had captured them and had apparently never gone through them. So when we put them on our computers and started looking at that material we recognised that what we were seeing were digital backup copies of the communications of the 28th Division that were sent to 2 Corps and the return flow. So, again, that further enforced the idea that the 28th Infantry Division was fully performing in a military manner, had not disarmed, and was conducting armed combat operations. So, again, in specific terms those opinions were formed well before General Krstic was indicted in -- was it late 1998 or early 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And had they been part of your reports and your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should pause a moment after the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have those opinions been part of your reports and testimony since you first developed them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I've never changed my opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in response to General Tolimir's questions about the demilitarisation or lack thereof, and I don't want you to get into this in-depth, but I just think it would be fair to touch upon it: Given the small numbers that the UN put for UN troops in the enclave to deal with the population and the issues related to those resolutions, was it -- in this war in 1993, would it -- was it reasonable to expect the Muslims not to harm themselves in some way or to try to have some way to protect themselves against the Serb army that was surrounding them? And I just want this to be very short. I don't want to take sides in this -- in this case that is really not disputed on this issue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the context of the allegations of Bosnian Muslim atrocities against the Serbs which occurred in late 1992 and early 1993, particularly related to Kravica in January 1993 and other massacres, had it occurred, that were blamed on the Bosnian Muslims, their understanding of the situation was that they felt they had to defend themselves because if they were ever captured by the Bosnian Serbs there would be some form of retribution for what they had done or what they were accused to have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get back to where we were. You said you had reviewed some of these BiH documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 411.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll -- we see it's from the Army of the Republic of the BH, 28th Division Command, Srebrenica, dated 5 July. And it's in the name of the Chief of Staff standing in for the commander, and the Chief of Staff is Major Ramiz Becirovic. It's a combat report. And to make things -- is this basically a Muslim version of the combat report that we've seen so many of from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the part of it I want to put your attention to is entitled: "Humanitarian Situation." Had you reviewed this set of documents, the combat reports from July 5th through the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And looking at - and I won't read it -- but the description of the humanitarian situation, and does that support the -- well, the issue in the UN report and the other contention that their -- the Muslim civilian population was facing a humanitarian hunger situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 411 shall be assigned Exhibit P2578. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I want to go through, again, but I don't need to spend much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 413. It's the -- another combat report from Becirovic of 6 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It points out the elderly and weak persons are an exceptionally difficult situation, due to starvation. We can see the rest of it. Is this another document you reviewed on the same topic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 413 shall be assigned Exhibit P2579. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And 65 ter 414, dated 7 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, looking at the humanitarian section on the bottom of the first page, top of the second page in English. Same thing in B/C/S. Is this another document you related -- you reviewed for the same subject?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would have seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 414 shall be assigned Exhibit P2580. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now let's go to 415. Same kind of document, dated 8 July. If we could go to page 2 in the English, and it would be page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see here that it -- there's a similar situation, but it also -- Becirovic mentions that it is necessary to do everything to get the international community to prevention a military and humanitarian catastrophe. So he makes a specifying reference to the military needing this material as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does this -- what does this say about Becirovic's knowledge about the military getting access to humanitarian aid that's coming in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it was known by everyone, including the Chief of Staff, that the 28th Division was taking a slice of the humanitarian aid to feed its own soldiers. The problem, of course, that he has here is that with no humanitarian aid there is no slice for him to take, and he's noting the fact that, you know, they are down to their last few days, and not even the army at this point is going to have adequate food supplies for the troops on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 415 shall be assigned Exhibit P2581. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the last document on this topic, 65 ter 416. And if we could -- we see it's a 9 July report of Ramiz Becirovic. And go to the second page in English, and we stay at the first page in the B/C/S, initially. So if we could go to the -- for this 9 July document go to the second page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again we see him saying -- now he's saying the humanitarian situation is catastrophic. The population and soldiers have no food reserves. So is this similar to the previous one he's now making -- he's again making specific reference to soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 416 shall be assigned Exhibit P2582. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go to -- if we could get D41 on briefly. It's the 9 July document under General Tolimir's name, noting that President Karadzic had agreed with the proposal to go forward and take Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General Tolimir asked you about this beginning page 17297. And he asked you at 17928: "Can you answer this question: General Tolimir, as a signatory of this document, did he not openly write about war crimes and propose public measures aimed at preventing those from happening at the same time as these measures are carried out?" And then he goes on the next question continuing to talk about this: "Are security organs here referring to what the lawful conduct of these units should be? Aren't they publicly pointing their finger at these issues or are they conceal and expressing these facts in the documents sent out to the various units?" And you answer his questions, but you do not refer to his comment and regarding this particular document and regarding whether or not you felt this is a public document. Is his reference to that this is happening publicly and that this is publicly pointing this out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we have D41 on the screen. Is this -- D41, is this a public document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that we have a wrong document on the screen. There seems to have been an error in the transcript. Now we have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when the General says, "Aren't the security branch," I guess he's referring to himself here, "Aren't they publicly pointing out their finger at these issues?" So is this document that we see here public?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that when I responded to General Tolimir on this I noted the fact that this is not a public document that's openly disclosed. This is a confidential military document. It notes "strictly confidential" on it. So while within the context of the military those individuals who are cleared to see the document would see the document, it's not a public document in the sense that it's going to make its way into, you know, the media, or things of that nature. I mean, this is a classified military document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I have one more section to go. So I am getting more confident at this point that we will be able to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have our second break now, and we will resume quater past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I think you will recall that you and General Tolimir discussed at length your view of his authority to prevent war crimes, to investigate the security branch's responsibility to investigate war crimes, and at page 17387 he asked you this: "My question is this: Did the Main Staff carry out an investigation on the crimes comitted in Srebrenica? Did an investigation take place after that?" And you said: "No, sir. No meaningful investigation was taken by the Main Staff, to my knowledge." And then there is a brief reference to Beara. Do you recall in your narrative did you deal with this subject and identify some documents related to this area of whether or not an investigation was carried out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's briefly go over some of the these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this first note we'll see is from the Republika Srpska military prosecutor's office, dated 26 March 1996, and it says in handwriting: "Notice from the VRS Military Prosecutor's Office to the Main Staff of the establishment of a commission for the exhumation of bodies." And it's in the name of military prosecutor Major Predrag Drinic. And there's some stamps on it. And it says on the next page in the English, and I think we should go to the next page on the B/C/S, as well. A handwritten note: "Order of the president of the republic, confidential," and the number 23 March. And then the next page of the document, if we could go to that. Both languages. And now we see the basically the same date, and it's the Military Prosecutor's Office still, Zvornik, 26 March, 1996. And we can see that it's to the VRS Main Staff, the department of intelligence and security affairs. And then if we briefly scan it we can see that the prosecutor had been informed that a mixed military and civilian commission for the exhumation of bodies in the area of the village of Pilica had been established with the co-operation of a forensic medicine and pathology expert. And it talks about the commission and a meeting and that Duty Operative Milorad Trbic attended the meeting on behalf of the Zvornik Brigade. Can you remind us who Milorad Trbic is or was at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He was the assistant to Drago Nikolic. So he was the deputy of Drago Nikolic, the chief of security for the Drina Corps. He was his number two person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this military prosecutor, Major Predrag Drinic, do you remember what he was the military prosecutor for, what area or ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the eastern Bosnia area. If I recall correctly, he was -- in July 1995 there was the -- the military prosecutor was in Zvornik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he -- Drinic, as we see here, goes to this meeting, and reports, and he says, and I quote: "None of the people present knew any details of the locality and of the actions that needed to be undertaken. Nor was anyone informed about what would be found on the site, or else no one wanted to know." And then it says: "In view of this state of affairs, I propose ..." And then he proposes a three-part -- a three-member part of commission of intelligence and security organ who would obtain accurate information about the above mentioned order of the president. And we see that after obtaining information, if the matter is in the competence of the military judicial organs, the competent military prosecutor and investigating judge must be informed immediately. And then we see it's signed and stamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page where we have another version of this same document. Which is -- says the same thing, but we see handwritten up in the right-hand corner: "For Beara."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where these two documents came from, why one has this "for Beara" on it and the other doesn't? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, this set of documents was found during a search of the archives of the RS MOD in Banja Luka. All these documents were found in one particular file, one of them said handwritten "to Beara," the other ones did not. I don't recall what the difference was. I think when the files were consolidated, one copy that went to the Main Staff had writing on it, and a copy from Mr. Drinic obviously didn't go to the Main Staff and it didn't have the writing on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, apparently on the back of the document we have written with the initials: "After the fax was sent, no answer was received from the Main Staff." And then we see those same initials that if we go back to the previous page for the signature of Drinic, on the original. In any event, what do you make of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This supports my phrase that there was no meaningful investigation undertaken. Both in the case of Milorad Trbic and Colonel Beara, both of them were well aware of what had happened at Pilica and when it had occurred, and I think the paragraph or phrase which lays it out the best was they are looking for guidance on not only -- you know, they didn't know what was supposed to be, quote, "found there," and nobody wanted to know what was going to be found there. Everyone knew what was there. So, again, they were reacting to the RS president's orders to investigate, but it wasn't a meaningful investigation. And the investigation, when one looks at the investigative file, it stops at the end of this document. There are no additional reports from the military prosecutor or the investigative judge. There are no witness statements. It dies at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page in the series of documents. Okay. We've seen that. Let's go on to the next one. Now, I believe there had been a reference in the previous document. And we now see an order from the -- from Karadzic. And this is dated March 23rd. And we see a reference to an order of President Karadzic in the previous Drinic document, which was number 01-445/96 of 23 March, 1996. So this apparently is a copy of that order referred to by Drinic, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what is this order by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order, again, is reacting to the alleged discovery of decomposing bodies at the scene of earlier battles with the Muslim side in the Pilica area, and they have also -- or, basically, what the president is ordering, both the military organs as well as the MUP, to conduct an investigation and report back to the president of the republic. The previous documents were the military's version of that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we note that earlier battles with the Muslim side in the Pilica area, have you discussed this in detail previously in your direct testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just remind us what you said about Pilica and where it was in relation to the battle-front and any battles?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pilica was in the zone of the 1st Infantry Battalion, well to the north of the places where the column went through and where the battle took place. So in July of 1995, there was no combat occurring at Pilica. Consequently, there are no battle casualties from Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is also a reference we see here that -- to Madeleine Albright, and you have also mentioned Madeleine Albright, I believe, and her publication of photos in the Pilica area and before the UN in New York. Can you -- again, does this have anything to do with that previous testimony, this reference, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They are aware that, like everybody else, that in August of 1995, at the United Nations the United States representative to the UN Security Council, Ms. Albright, laid out a series of overhead imagery products which reflected, particularly in the Pilica area, and Branjevo, the fact that hundreds of individuals had been killed and were being subsequently buried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence, this series of documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 65 ter 519 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 519 shall be assigned Exhibit P2583. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now go to 65 ter 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this another one of the documents you recall analysing and discussing in the past? Take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see that it's -- it's from the President Radovan Karadzic. It's to the Main Staff and several other addressees. And it's saying: "Pursuant to Article 80 of the Constitution of Republika Srpska, I hereby order," and it talks about ordering a detailed investigation into the locations where the victims of armed conflict in and around Srebrenica are to be found. And as we can see, it talks about finding them, trying to identify the cause of death and the circumstances relevant to their demise. Paragraph 2 says it should be properly investigated, especially the intentional murder of civilians. It mentions the Geneva Conventions and identifying the perpetrators so that proceedings can be brought, and it should be implemented by, and then they list the Main Staff of the VRS, the minister of defence/interior and various other folks, including the military prosecutor. Do you remember whether or not they -- there was a document reflecting the results of that investigation order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that Dragomir Vasic, the head of CSB Zvornik did, in fact, put together a response to this document with respect to the results of his investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this document 65 ter 21 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 21 shall be assigned Exhibit P2584. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could now go to 65 ter 23. And I think it -- we need to start with -- now, let's see, it may be page 2 that we need to start with. No, that looks right in the B/C/S. Now the -- yeah, we need to go to page 2 in the English. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we see that this is from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Interior, office of the minister in Pale, 23 September 1996. Ministry of Justice and Administration, Mr. Goran Neskovic, and: "Enclosed a report of the Ministry of the Interior with information concerning the period when Srebrenica was liberated." Minister Dragan Kijac. So let's go to the next page, and maybe the previous page in English. It should be page 2 in the B/C/S. Just in scanning this, Mr. Butler, does this look like the report you were referring to? And take your time. This is the last document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mention Dragomir Vasic. Do you see him on this anywhere or ...?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't see his name on this particular page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so if we see this report of the Ministry of the Interior, how is this document, in your view, related to the -- Karadzic's request for investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first paragraph, essentially, lays out the situation; whereas, their view was that most of casualties that are being viewed here are, in fact, Muslims killing themselves for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you referring to the -- when it says: [As read] "... Buljim-Konjevic Polje-Cerska-Kamenica-Baljkovica stretch, there were several individual and mass killings among the Muslims."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, "Those killings were organised by senior officers ..." Is that -- senior officers of which army, as far as you can tell from the way this is written?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the ABiH army. And then, of course, the fourth paragraph down they are already working to potentially discredit testimony of at least one of them, Mevludin Oric, who was a survivor from, I believe, the Orahovac execution, if I recall correctly. So they can work on discrediting that as well as, you know, providing information on what they think the Tribunal is looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mevludin Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, aside from this President Karadzic order for investigation, and this to the minister of justice, among others, and this brief report on the Srebrenica conclusions that the Muslims did this to themselves, among others things, were you aware of any other indications of any investigation or review by the VRS or RS during the time-frame of the war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time-frame of the war and the period shortly thereafter, this is it. I don't believe that the RS ever investigated the issue with respect to Srebrenica until perhaps 2002 or 2003 when the RS commission responsible for investigating Srebrenica published their initial report, which was then subsequently withdrawn and rewritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would then offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please see the last page with the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If there is any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's it, Mr. President. No signature block on what we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 23 shall be assigned Exhibit P2585. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. It's even quarter before 7.00. Mr. Butler, the Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and that you have provided us with your expertise as a result of your review of your documents. It was a long time since the beginning of July, with a break in between. Thank you very much for your patience, and it was very helpful for both parties and the Chamber that you were able to come here and to testify. Now you are free to return to your normal activities and to your home. And again, thank you very much, and a safe trip home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and I appreciate the time and patience that the Trial Chamber has had with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Everybody was patient, indeed. We have to adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we have some minutes left, the Registrar has to put something on the record in relation to one document -- or two documents. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On 25th of August, 2011, the Registry was instructed to attach the transcript under 65 ter 1D217 to an Exhibit P2125. Considering that this 65 ter document was already part of an exhibit, D72, the transcript has been uploaded by the Prosecution and subsequently has been attached to Exhibit P2125. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And that was related to transcript of a video-clip we have seen in the courtroom. We have to adjourn for the day. It's not sensible to start with the next witness. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of September, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.47 p.m.
